lesson.title: Correlation is not a cause

lead.text: The clerk's lists are easier to read as a picture. Draw a sheet with the day's takings along the bottom and its rescues up the side, and put one dot for each day where its two figures meet. A day with big takings and many rescues lands far to the right and high up. A day with small takings and few rescues lands near the bottom left.

In the town's picture the dots climb from the lower left to the upper right. This pattern, where two measures tend to rise and fall together, is called a correlation. Because both measures rise, it is a positive one.

afterFigure.text: The second picture shows the opposite pattern. People were asked how many hours they had slept and then timed on how quickly they reacted to a light, and the dots slide downhill. Reaction time is a time, so a smaller number means a quicker person. People who slept more were quicker, so one measure falls as the other rises. That is a negative correlation.
A pattern like this is easy to see but hard to describe exactly. The next screen gives a way to say how tight it is without waving a hand at the picture.

lead.text: A picture shows a pattern, but two people can disagree about how strong it looks. Statisticians settle that with one number, the correlation coefficient, written r. It is worked out from the dots, and it always lies between −1 and +1.

Two things about r matter. Its sign gives the direction. A plus sign means the measures rise together, as in the town, where r is +0.75. A minus sign means one falls as the other rises. Its size, with the sign ignored, gives the strength. At +1 or −1 every dot sits exactly on a straight line, and at 0 there is no line to see, only a cloud. The nearer r is to either end of the scale, the more tightly the dots follow a line.

afterFigure.text: Compare the two pictures. The town's dots hug a rising line, and r = +0.75. The dots for practice and test score are more spread out, and r = +0.4. Both slope upward, and the larger number marks the tighter pattern.
So r tells you which way the dots lean and how closely they follow a line. It says nothing about why they lean that way, and that question is where the rest of the lesson goes.

lead.text: Direction and strength are separate things. Use what the last screen said about each when you compare these two correlations.

Strength can also be put another way. The kiosk's takings change from day to day, and that spread is the variation in the takings. The rescues vary too. Where two measures are correlated, part of the variation in one goes along with the variation in the other.

To find out how large that part is, square r. The result is the share of the variation the two measures have in common, called the shared variation. With r = 0.4 the square is 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16, so the two lists share 16% of their variation. The other 84% belongs to things that do not line up with the other list.

Squaring also removes the sign, because a negative number times itself is positive. A correlation of −0.4 shares exactly as much as +0.4, since direction has no bearing on how much two lists have in common. A correlation that looks respectable at 0.4 still leaves most of the variation unshared.
Here are the sleep and reaction-time dots again. The first picture has a correlation of r = −0.6.
Back to the clerk's records. Takings and rescues rise and fall together across the summer, and nobody has said why. Use what you know about a seaside town in summer.

The answer you chose is the most common reason two lists match when neither causes the other. On hot days the kiosk sells more ice cream, and on hot days the pool is crowded, so there are more swimmers and more chances for one to get into difficulty. Heat sits behind both lists and pushes them up together. A hidden variable that drives both measures like this is called a confound.
You can test for a confound by holding it still. The clerk also wrote down each day's temperature, and the first picture shades every dot by it. The high-takings, high-rescue days are the hot ones.

afterFigure.text: The second picture keeps only days of about the same temperature, between 21 and 23 °C. With the temperature held still, the upward lean has gone: higher takings no longer go with more rescues, and r falls from +0.75 to about 0.

So the kiosk was never sending anyone into the water, because the weather drove both lists. That is why a correlation alone cannot show a cause: the dots show a pattern, but what lies behind it may be a variable nobody wrote down.

lead.text: Confounds turn up wherever two measures both depend on something else, as both lists in the town depended on the weather.

A confound is one way to explain a match, and the direction of the link is another. When exercise and mood go together, it is natural to say that exercise lifts mood, but the numbers cannot confirm that. A correlation is symmetric: swap the two axes of the picture and r stays exactly the same.
The figure draws one study of exercise and mood both ways round, with r = +0.3 in each.

afterFigure.text: The data look identical either way, so nothing in them says which measure is the cause. People who feel good may be the ones who go for a run. Putting the arrow the other way, from mood to exercise, is called reverse causation. Both directions can even hold at once.
To separate them you would have to decide who exercises, instead of watching who chooses to. The next lesson is about doing exactly that.

lead.text: Each explanation below says something different about why exercise and mood go together.

The third way a match can arise is in the mind of the person looking. A driver says it always rains the day after he washes his car. He remembers the rainy times because they annoyed him, and he forgets the dry times, which he never gave a thought. To test his belief you have to count every day, not only the memorable ones.

Say he washed the car on 10 days and it rained after 4 of them. On the other 90 days it rained after 36. The counts are different sizes, so turn each into a percentage first: 4 out of 10 is 40%, and 36 out of 90 is also 40%. Rain followed a wash no more often than it followed anything else.

afterFigure.text: Believing in a link that the full counts do not show is called an illusory correlation. It grows from vivid cases, which are easy to remember. The cure is to count the dull cases too and compare rates in every group.

lead.text: Hospital staff swear their emergency department is busier under a full moon. They remember the chaotic full-moon shifts. The counts for every shift are in the picture.

model.setting: Emergency-department shifts under a full moon

lesson.orientation: Read the sign and strength of a correlation, then look for what else could produce it.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A seaside town keeps two sets of records through the summer. The ice-cream kiosk on the front writes down its takings each day. The lifeguards at the open-air pool write down each swimmer they have to pull out of trouble. At the end of the season a council clerk puts the two lists side by side and sees that they follow each other. The days with the biggest takings are the days with the most rescues, and the quiet days are quiet for both.

At the next meeting a councillor proposes closing the kiosk, since it seems to be sending people into trouble in the water. The clerk is not sure. A matching pattern in two lists is easy to see, but it does not say what produced it.

This lesson follows the clerk's records from the pattern itself to the question of what lies behind it. We start by drawing the pattern and putting a number on how closely two lists match. Then we look at the different ways a match can arise, some of which have nothing to do with one thing causing the other.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure how closely two things move together and name three ways they can match without a cause.

recap.keyIdea: A correlation gives direction, strength and shared variation, but never the cause. A confound, a reversed arrow or a vivid memory can each produce a pattern that nothing causes.

blocks.text: Back at the seaside, the clerk has what the council lacked. Takings and rescues had r = +0.75, and with the weather held still the link vanished, so the kiosk can stay open. You squared r = −0.6 to find that sleep and reaction time share 36% of their variation, and you found that 6 of 20 and 30 of 100 are the same busy rate.

recap.nextHook: A correlation cannot say which explanation is right, but a study that decides for itself who gets what can, and the next lesson begins with a gym that lets its members choose.

questions.prompt: Daily screen time and sleep quality correlate at r = −0.3. What percentage of the variation in sleep quality is shared with screen time?
hints: Use the square of the correlation coefficient.
The minus sign disappears when you square.
Square 0.3 and convert to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: r² = 0.3² = 0.09, so 9%. A modest correlation leaves 91% of the variation to other causes.

questions.onCorrect: Square r and the sign drops out. A modest correlation shares only a small slice of the variation.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads r as a percentage. Square it first.
That is the share left over, not the share they have in common.

questions.prompt: Across towns, those with more libraries also have more burglaries. Population size drives both. What do psychologists call a variable like population that produces a misleading correlation?
hints: It is a hidden third variable that affects both measured variables.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Population is a confound: a third variable that drives both measures.

questions.onCorrect: A confound drives both measures, so they move together without either causing the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Reverse causation flips the arrow between two measures. Here a separate variable sits behind both.

questions.prompt: A teacher recalls that rainy days bring rowdy classes. Counted properly, 9 of 30 rainy days were rowdy and 40 of 100 dry days were. By how many percentage points is the rowdy rate higher on dry days?
hints: Turn each count into a rate.
Divide the rowdy days by all days in each group.
Subtract the smaller rate from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9/30 = 30% and 40/100 = 40%, so the gap is 40 − 30 = 10 percentage points.

questions.onCorrect: Compare rates in every group. The rainy days only felt more rowdy.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the raw counts, but the groups differ in size. Turn each count into a rate first.
That is one of the rates, not the gap between them.

questions.prompt: Ice-cream takings and pool rescues in a seaside town rise and fall together through the summer. What best explains why?
hints: Ask what else changes across the year.
Sales and rescues are both highest in the same weeks. What do those weeks have in common?

acceptedIdeas: Hot weather brings more people to both the ice-cream van and the pool.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hot weather: it brings more people to the ice-cream van and to the pool.

choices.label: Eating ice cream makes swimmers more likely to need rescuing.
Hot weather brings more people to both the ice-cream van and the pool.
Rescues make onlookers want ice cream.

questions.onCorrect: Something outside both lists moves them together. The next screen gives that hidden driver a name.

misconceptions.feedback: Possible, but the pattern alone does not show it. Ask what else changes through the year.
That reverses the arrow, and nothing in the pattern points that way. Look for something that changes both.

questions.prompt: Is a correlation of r = −0.6 stronger or weaker than one of r = +0.4?
hints: Strength is the distance from zero. Ignore the sign when you compare.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stronger: r = −0.6 is further from zero. The minus sign only gives direction.

questions.onCorrect: Strength is distance from zero, so −0.6 is stronger than +0.4. The sign only gives the direction.

misconceptions.feedback: A plus sign shows direction, not strength. Compare the sizes with the signs set aside.

questions.prompt: Two measures correlate at r = 0.5. What percentage of their variation do they have in common?
hints: Squaring r gives the shared share.
Multiply 0.5 by itself.
Convert the decimal to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: r² = 0.5² = 0.25, so 25% of the variation is shared.

questions.onCorrect: Square r, then read it as a percentage: 0.5 × 0.5 is a quarter, or 25%.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads r as a percentage. The share comes from squaring it first.
That divides r by ten rather than squaring it.

questions.prompt: Sleep and reaction time correlate at r = −0.6. What percentage of the variation in reaction time do they share?
hints: The shared share of variation comes from squaring r.
A negative number squared is positive.
Square 0.6 and convert the decimal to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Shared variance is r² = (−0.6)² = 0.36, so 36%. Squaring removes the sign.

questions.onCorrect: Squaring r removes the sign: (−0.6)² gives the shared share, a little over a third of the variation.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads r as a percentage. The shared share comes from squaring r.
That is the right square written as a decimal. The question asks for a percentage.
That is the share left over. The question asks how much is shared.

questions.prompt: Children with bigger shoe sizes read better. Name the most likely confound.
hints: A confound is a third variable that drives both measures. What changes both shoe size and reading skill?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Age drives both measures: older children have bigger feet and better reading.

questions.onCorrect: Age moves both measures together. A confound sits behind the pattern, not between the two measures.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the two measures. The question asks for a third variable behind both.

questions.prompt: Why does holding temperature roughly fixed make the link disappear?
hints: What changed from day to day in the first picture? What changes in the second?

acceptedIdeas: Temperature was what moved sales and rescues together, so once it is fixed nothing is left to move them together.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Temperature moved both measures; fixed, it cannot.

choices.label: Ice-cream sales stop mattering once the days are warm.
A smaller set of days always shows a weaker correlation.
Temperature was what moved sales and rescues together, so once it is fixed nothing is left to move them together.

questions.onCorrect: Fixing the confound removes what linked the two measures. That is what a confound does.

misconceptions.feedback: Sales never mattered to rescues in the first place. The question is what linked them.
Fewer days alone do not weaken a real link. Something specific stopped the pattern.

questions.prompt: Across a sample, weekly exercise and mood correlate at r = 0.3. Which explanation has the arrow running from mood to exercise?
hints: Reverse causation flips which variable is the cause.

acceptedIdeas: People in a better mood are more likely to go out and exercise
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reverse causation runs the arrow from mood to exercise. Sunny weather would be a confound, and endorphins assume the original direction.

choices.label: People in a better mood are more likely to go out and exercise
Exercise raises mood by releasing endorphins
Sunny weather increases both exercise and mood

questions.onCorrect: When the arrow runs from mood to exercise, being in a good mood leads to more exercise. The correlation alone cannot rule it out.

misconceptions.feedback: That has the arrow running from exercise to mood, the direction the data seem to suggest.
That puts a third variable behind both measures. No arrow runs between exercise and mood.

questions.prompt: 6 of 20 full-moon shifts were busy, and 30 of 100 other shifts were busy. By how many percentage points does the busy rate differ between the two kinds of shift?
hints: Turn each count into a rate before comparing.
Divide busy shifts by all shifts in each group.
Subtract one rate from the other.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6/20 = 30% and 30/100 = 30%, so the difference is 0 percentage points. The remembered link is an illusory correlation.

questions.onCorrect: Both groups were busy at the same rate. The vivid full-moon nights were memorable, not more frequent.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts raw counts, but the groups differ in size. Turn each into a rate first.
That compares the quiet shifts, which are different in number. Compare rates, not counts.
